guide.title: Theater District, Manhattan: From Longacre Square to the Great White Way
guide.intro: Longacre Square, named for London's carriage-trade district, became Times Square on April 8, 1904, when The New York Times moved into a new tower there — but the theater district around it had already taken shape two decades earlier, after the Metropolitan Opera House relocated to West 39th Street in 1883 and Oscar Hammerstein I opened his Victoria Theatre on 42nd Street in 1899. Electric arc lamps installed in the 1880s gave Broadway its nickname, "The Great White Way," as the district moved uptown. The first New Year's Eve ball drop took place December 31, 1907, and has continued nearly every year since, save 1942 and 1943, when wartime lighting restrictions suspended it. After a decline into adult entertainment in the 1970s, 1990s revitalization brought back the crowds; the Lyceum Theatre became the first landmarked Broadway theater in 1974, and 28 theaters held landmark status by 1988.

sections.heading: From Longacre Square to the Great White Way
sections.body: The area was Longacre Square, named after London's horse-and-carriage district, until it was renamed Times Square on April 8, 1904, when publisher Adolph S. Ochs moved The New York Times into a new tower there (now One Times Square). The theater district itself had begun taking shape two decades earlier: the Metropolitan Opera House moved to West 39th Street in 1883, drawing theaters and restaurants uptown, and Oscar Hammerstein I opened his Victoria Theatre on 42nd Street in 1899, the same era the subway's first line was under construction (it opened in 1904). Broadway's "Great White Way" nickname dates to 1880s electric arc-lamp illumination and stuck as the district moved uptown. After decades of decline into adult entertainment through the 1970s, the district was revitalized in the 1990s: preservation campaigns made the Lyceum Theatre the first landmarked Broadway theater in 1974, and 28 theaters had landmark status by 1988.

sections.heading: A Pedestrian Times Square
sections.body: Broadway's traffic lanes through Times Square, between 42nd and 47th Streets, were closed to cars in a 2009 trial under Mayor Bloomberg and made a permanent pedestrian plaza in February 2010, with a granite-paver redesign completed just before New Year's Eve 2016. The move transformed the crossroads long associated with December 31 ball drops — a tradition dating to 1907, suspended only in 1942 and 1943 for wartime lighting restrictions — into a year-round pedestrian stage for performers, vendors, and Times Square Alliance programming.

sections.heading: Getting there by subway
sections.body: The district centers on two of the system's busiest hubs: Times Sq-42 St, served by the 1/2/3, 7, N/Q/R/W, and the 42nd Street shuttle (S), and 42 St-Port Authority Bus Terminal, served by the A/C/E, connected to Times Square by an underground passage. Note that the W runs weekdays only, and the R and the S shuttle skip late nights.

faq.question: How do I get to the Theater District by subway?
faq.answer: Times Sq-42 St is served by the 1/2/3, 7, N/Q/R/W, and the 42nd Street shuttle (S); 42 St-Port Authority Bus Terminal is served by the A/C/E and connects to Times Square by an underground passage. The W runs weekdays only, and the R and S shuttle skip late nights.

faq.question: When did Times Square get its name?
faq.answer: The area was originally Longacre Square, named after London's carriage-trade district. It was renamed Times Square on April 8, 1904, after publisher Adolph S. Ochs moved The New York Times into a new tower there.

faq.question: Where can I get discount Broadway tickets?
faq.answer: The TKTS booth in Duffy Square, at Broadway and West 47th Street, has sold same-day discount tickets since June 1973. Hours vary by day: Wednesday, Thursday, Saturday, and Sunday from 11 a.m., Monday, Tuesday, and Friday from 3 p.m., all until 8 p.m.

faq.question: How long has the Times Square ball drop been happening?
faq.answer: The first ball drop took place December 31, 1907, and has continued nearly every year since, with the exception of 1942 and 1943, when wartime lighting restrictions suspended it.

faq.question: Where can I stay in the Theater District?
faq.answer: Hotel Edison, a 1931 hotel where Thomas Edison himself turned on the lights at opening, and Paramount Times Square - A Generator Hotel, with its Broadway Tuesdays live-events series, are both verified in-neighborhood options.

places.name: Duffy Square & TKTS Booth
places.address: Broadway at West 47th Street, New York, NY 10036
places.summary: The northern triangle of Times Square, dedicated in June 1939 to honor WWI chaplain Father Francis P. Duffy; the TKTS discount booth has sold same-day Broadway tickets there since June 1973, with hours varying by day (Wednesday, Thursday, Saturday, and Sunday from 11 a.m.; Monday, Tuesday, and Friday from 3 p.m.; all until 8 p.m.).

places.name: New Amsterdam Theatre
places.summary: Opened October 26, 1903, and home to the Ziegfeld Follies through much of 1913-1927; Disney restored the theater 1995-1997, and its Beaux-Arts exterior and Art Nouveau interior were designated New York City landmarks in 1979 and listed on the National Register in 1980. Now operated by Disney Theatrical Group, home to the musical Aladdin.

places.name: Lyceum Theatre
places.summary: Opened in 1903 to a Beaux-Arts design by Herts & Tallant, Broadway's oldest continually operating legitimate theatre and, in 1974, the first Broadway theater to receive New York City landmark status.

places.name: Madame Tussauds New York
places.summary: Wax museum with over 200 figures across five themed floors, open daily 10 a.m. to 9 p.m., with tickets from $34.

places.name: Joe Allen
places.summary: A pre- and post-theater dining institution on Restaurant Row since 1965. Closed annually for a late-August summer break; reservations via OpenTable.

places.name: Carmine's Times Square
places.summary: Family-style Southern Italian restaurant known for its huge shared platters, open daily until 11 p.m. (midnight Friday and Saturday).

places.name: John's of Times Square
places.summary: Coal-fired brick-oven pizzeria operating for over 28 years inside a restored 19th-century former church, complete with stained glass and a large skylight.

places.name: Junior's Restaurant & Bakery (West 45th Street)
places.address: 1515 Broadway at West 45th Street, New York, NY 10036
places.summary: Brooklyn original founded in 1950, famous for its cheesecake made from a five-ingredient recipe unchanged since founding; this Times Square location is one of two Manhattan restaurants.

places.name: Hotel Edison
places.summary: A 26-story hotel opened in 1931, designed by Herbert J. Krapp, with Thomas Edison himself turning on the lights at its opening; home to the Rum House bar.

places.name: Paramount Times Square (A Generator Hotel)
places.summary: Historic Theater District hotel operated as a Generator property, with an in-house bar, restaurant, and a Broadway Tuesdays live-events series in the lobby.
